antiseptic

/an-tih-SEP-tik/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Antiseptic means clean and free of harmful germs.

The tattoo artist wiped the skin with an antiseptic solution before uncapping a fresh needle.

Example

Before the tour group entered the bottling room, each visitor scrubbed to the elbow and put on gloves, a hairnet, and shoe covers. Inside, stainless-steel tanks gleamed under white light, and the air itself carried the faint tang of the cleaning rinse. The guide explained that the entire room was kept antiseptic: one stray microbe could spoil ten thousand bottles of juice.

The scrubbing, gloves, and rigorously germ-free environment — maintained so that not one microbe survives — show exactly what antiseptic means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sanitized: Sanitized means cleaned so that microbes have been removed or killed, and it reports a job already done — a gym mat sanitized at closing time. Antiseptic describes the ongoing state that such cleaning aims at: kept free of harmful germs, usually to stop infection before it starts.

germ-free: Germ-free simply states the result: no harmful microbes are present, however that came about. Antiseptic carries the medical purpose behind that state — wipes, solutions, and spaces deliberately kept germ-free to prevent infection. High mountain air may happen to be germ-free; an antiseptic wipe is germ-free by design.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

contaminated: tainted with germs or impurities

germ-ridden: full of harmful microbes

Where it sits · how deep the cleanliness goes

tidy → antiseptic → sterile

tidy vs. antiseptic: A tidy room is merely neat to the eye, while an antiseptic one is free of the germs themselves.

sterile vs. antiseptic: Sterile is the extreme end of antiseptic — absolutely no living microbes at all, as on a surgical instrument.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — anti-: against (Greek)

Root — sept-: to rot (Greek sepein)

Suffix — -ic: relating to; having the quality of

Put it together: Antiseptic combines Greek anti-, 'against,' with sepein, 'to rot': literally 'against rotting.' The same root gives us septic (infected, rotting) and sepsis (a dangerous infection of the blood). September, despite its look, comes from Latin septem, 'seven' — an unrelated root.

Use the root in a new word: septic: A septic wound is one that has begun to rot with infection — from Greek sepein, 'to rot,' the same root hiding inside antiseptic.

Word Building

Word Choice

clinical, hygienic

Antiseptic describes wipes, solutions, and environments kept free of germs. Keep it apart from analgesic (another word in this unit): antiseptic keeps a wound free of germs, while an analgesic eases the pain — the two live side by side in a first-aid kit but never trade jobs.
